difficultyReason: The flaw is necessary/sufficient confusion — treating a sufficient condition as necessary. Two answer choices involve similar conditional language, requiring careful tracking of which direction the error runs.
stimulus: Whenever a patient is admitted to Riverside Hospital with acute appendicitis, the surgical team is immediately assembled. Dr. Lena Hartwick is a member of the surgical team, and she has just been called in. Therefore, a patient with acute appendicitis must have been admitted.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The city's emergency notification system is activated whenever a Category 3 hurricane makes landfall nearby. The notification system was just activated, so a Category 3 hurricane must have made landfall nearby.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All competitive swimmers train for at least two hours daily. Marcus trains for at least two hours daily. Therefore, Marcus is a competitive swimmer.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a building receives a historic preservation designation, its exterior cannot be altered. The facade of Alderton House has not been altered, so it must have received a historic preservation designation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every employee who passes the advanced certification exam receives a pay raise. Fatima passed the advanced certification exam. Therefore, Fatima will receive a pay raise.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whenever the municipal pool is closed for maintenance, the parks department sends an announcement to all residents. No announcement was sent this week, so the pool was not closed for maintenance this week.

explanations.correct: The stimulus infers that the only cause of the surgical team being assembled is acute appendicitis — it treats 'appendicitis → team assembled' as if it were 'team assembled → appendicitis,' confusing a sufficient condition for a necessary one. Choice A commits the same error: 'Category 3 hurricane → notification system activated' is treated as 'notification activated → Category 3 hurricane.' The sufficient condition is mistakenly read as the only possible cause.
explanations.A: Correct. Same flaw: the sufficient condition (hurricane) is treated as the necessary/only explanation for the effect (notification), mirroring the stimulus exactly.
explanations.B: This confuses a necessary condition ('at least two hours of training' is necessary for competitive swimmers) with a sufficient one — a slightly different directional error. The stimulus errs by reversing a sufficient condition, not by elevating a necessary condition.
explanations.C: Close trap. 'Historic designation → no alteration' is reversed to conclude designation from no alteration. This is structurally similar but the premise in the stimulus describes an action triggered by an event; here the conditional is a restriction, not a triggered response. Also, the conclusion is about an exterior feature being unaltered, making it a converse error on a prohibition rather than on an activating cause.
explanations.D: This is a valid modus ponens inference — no flaw. The employee passed the exam (sufficient condition met), so the consequent (pay raise) follows correctly.
explanations.E: This is a valid modus tollens inference — if the notification system is the necessary signal of closure, the absence of notification validly implies no closure. No flaw is committed.

difficultyReason: The flaw is correlation-to-causation. Two answer choices involve causal language in familiar domains; students must distinguish a genuine causal inference error from a valid statistical inference and from a different flaw (sampling bias).
stimulus: A study of school districts found that districts with more after-school tutoring programs tend to have higher average standardized test scores. Clearly, the tutoring programs are raising students' test scores.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neighborhoods with more coffee shops per capita also tend to have lower rates of unemployment. Coffee shops must therefore be creating jobs and reducing unemployment in those neighborhoods.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The regions of the country that consume the most olive oil also report the lowest rates of cardiovascular disease. Therefore, at least some of the people in those regions consume olive oil.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because the survey sample was drawn entirely from urban residents, its finding that most people support public transit funding cannot be reliably extended to rural residents.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sales of umbrellas rise every autumn. Therefore, umbrella purchases must be causing the seasonal change in weather that autumn brings.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every city that has adopted a congestion-pricing scheme has seen a reduction in downtown traffic. We can therefore predict that the next city to adopt congestion pricing will also see reduced downtown traffic.

explanations.correct: The stimulus observes a correlation between tutoring programs and test scores, then concludes the programs cause the scores to rise — ignoring that wealthier or better-resourced districts might independently produce both outcomes. Choice A does the same: it observes a correlation (more coffee shops, lower unemployment) and concludes the coffee shops are causing the employment benefit, ignoring that both variables could stem from a common cause (e.g., economic prosperity).
explanations.A: Correct. Observes a correlation and infers a specific causal direction without ruling out confounding variables — identical flaw to the stimulus.
explanations.B: This is a valid inference: 'regions consume the most' entails that some people in those regions consume olive oil. No flaw is present; it's merely weak existential reasoning from a known fact.
explanations.C: This correctly identifies a sampling-bias problem, which is a different flaw — failure of representativeness — not correlation-to-causation.
explanations.D: This is a reversed-causation error (umbrella sales causing weather), which is technically a correlation-causation flaw, but the causal direction is backwards and the conclusion is absurd rather than merely unwarranted. It differs from the stimulus in that the stimulus infers plausible-seeming causation from correlation; D infers implausible reverse causation. The closer match remains A.
explanations.E: This is an inductive generalization from past cases to a future case — a valid (though defeasible) predictive inference. No specific flaw in causal attribution is committed.

difficultyReason: The flaw is a part-to-whole (composition) fallacy. Three answer choices involve property-transfer reasoning; students must distinguish the composition fallacy from a valid generalization and from a division fallacy (whole-to-part).
stimulus: Each individual chapter of Professor Okafor's new linguistics textbook is concise and easy to follow. Therefore, the textbook as a whole must be concise and easy to follow.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every molecule of water is odorless and tasteless. Therefore, a glass of pure water must be odorless and tasteless.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The national economy is healthy and growing. Therefore, each sector of the economy must be healthy and growing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every ingredient in this stew was fresh when purchased. Therefore, this stew must be fresh and delicious.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Each musician in the chamber ensemble is a highly skilled soloist. Therefore, the ensemble's performances as a group must be outstanding.

choices.label: E
choices.text: This documentary film is engaging and informative. Therefore, each individual segment of the film must be engaging and informative.

explanations.correct: The stimulus attributes a property of each individual part (each chapter is concise and easy to follow) to the whole (the textbook). This is the composition fallacy. Choice D does the same: each individual musician is a skilled soloist (part-level property), so the ensemble as a whole must be outstanding (whole-level conclusion). Individual excellence does not guarantee collective excellence — ensemble performance requires coordination, balance, and interaction that go beyond individual skill.
explanations.A: This is actually a valid inference, not a flaw. Properties of individual water molecules (odorlessness, tastelessness) do aggregate to the bulk substance by the nature of molecular uniformity. No fallacy is committed.
explanations.B: This is the division fallacy — inferring a property of the parts from a property of the whole — the reverse of the composition fallacy in the stimulus. The stimulus argues from parts to whole; B argues from whole to parts.
explanations.C: Close trap. Inferring 'fresh and delicious' from 'each ingredient was fresh' does move from parts to whole, but the conclusion adds 'delicious,' which requires an evaluative leap beyond the stated premise. This mixes composition with an unsupported additional claim, making it a slightly different error. More importantly, freshness genuinely does aggregate (fresh ingredients → fresh stew is at least partially valid), diluting the fallacy. D's error is purer.
explanations.D: Correct. Pure composition fallacy: individual skill (part) attributed to ensemble quality (whole), ignoring that group performance is an emergent, non-additive property.
explanations.E: This is the division fallacy — inferring properties of each segment from properties of the whole film — the reverse of the composition fallacy in the stimulus.
